package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it establishes a persistent, encrypted two-way communication channel with a remote command-and-control (C2) server upon installation, exfiltrates host and machine identifiers, and executes attacker-supplied, encrypted JavaScript payloads on the victim's machine. The package employs obfuscation, background daemonization, and anti-analysis techniques to evade detection and enable remote code execution, posing a severe risk to any system where it is installed.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At postinstall, the code executes index.js automatically upon package installation, launching the malicious payload and initiating the attack chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automatically executing code on install is a common malware technique to ensure immediate execution without user interaction, increasing the risk of compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages rarely require postinstall scripts unless for build or setup; here, it is used solely to trigger malware execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages use postinstall for compiling native modules or setup tasks, but not for launching persistent background processes.
key_indicators: postinstall script launching custom Node.js code
no legitimate installation/setup reason for script execution

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At postinstall, the code uses pm2 to launch app.js as a persistent, background daemon in cluster mode, ensuring the malicious process remains running and is automatically restarted if terminated.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Spawning a background daemon on install is highly unusual and enables persistent malicious activity, making the malware resilient to process termination.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not install persistent background processes on developer machines during installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: pm2 is used legitimately to manage Node.js services in production environments, but not during package installation on end-user or developer systems.
key_indicators: pm2 used to daemonize a script at install time
background process persistence initiated by package install

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code dynamically generates an AES encryption key and a C2 server URL using obfuscated logic, concealing static configuration and making static analysis and detection more difficult.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscated generation of keys and URLs is a hallmark of malware attempting to evade detection and analysis by hiding critical infrastructure details.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not obfuscate static configuration like keys or URLs, as this hinders maintainability and transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in proprietary software to protect intellectual property, but not for C2 infrastructure in open-source packages.
key_indicators: obfuscated string construction for keys and URLs
dynamic C2 URL and key generation at runtime

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Every 45 seconds at runtime, the code collects host and machine identifiers, encrypts them, and sends them to the C2 server; it then receives an encrypted payload, decodes and executes it using eval, enabling remote code execution by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Periodic exfiltration of host info and execution of remote, attacker-supplied code is highly malicious and enables full compromise of the victim system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not beacon to remote servers or execute arbitrary code received from the network.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Heartbeat mechanisms are used in legitimate monitoring agents, but never to execute arbitrary code from untrusted sources.
key_indicators: periodic network beaconing to C2 server
encrypted payload delivery and execution via eval
exfiltration of host and machine identifiers

execution_context.trigger: runtime (daemonized by pm2, on first run)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code checks for a marker file (node_logs.txt) in the temp directory; if absent, it creates the file and starts the heartbeat communication loop, using the file as a one-time execution token to control malicious logic.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of a hidden marker file to control execution flow is a stealth technique to avoid repeated execution and detection by security tools.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not use hidden marker files in temp directories to control malicious logic or execution flow.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Marker files may be used in installers to prevent duplicate runs, but not to gate malicious network activity.
key_indicators: hidden marker file (node_logs.txt) in temp directory
conditional execution of malicious logic based on file presence

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code encrypts all outbound and inbound C2 communications using AES-128-CBC, ensuring that network traffic between the infected host and the C2 server is not readable by network monitoring tools.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Custom encryption of C2 traffic is a strong indicator of malware attempting to evade network-based detection and forensic analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages rarely encrypt their own network traffic with custom keys and algorithms, especially for communication with unknown servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encryption is used in legitimate applications for secure communication, but not with hardcoded, obfuscated keys and C2 endpoints.
key_indicators: AES encryption of C2 traffic using custom key
encrypted payloads in network requests to C2 server

attack_chain.action: Upon installation, the postinstall script executes index.js.
index.js uses pm2 to launch app.js as a persistent background daemon.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious logic in app.js

attack_chain.action: app.js checks for a marker file and, if absent, creates it and starts the heartbeat loop.
Every 45 seconds, heartbeat collects host info and sends it (encrypted) to the C2 server.
attack_chain.leads_to: C2 server can respond with encrypted payloads

attack_chain.action: If a payload is received, it is decrypted, base64-decoded, and executed via eval, enabling remote code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves arbitrary code execution on victim machine

behavioral_signatures: postinstall script executing custom Node.js code during package installation
pm2 used to daemonize scripts at install time, creating persistent background processes
periodic (every 45 seconds) outbound HTTPS POST requests to hardcoded or obfuscated C2 domains
AES-encrypted payloads in network traffic between host and C2 server
eval execution of decrypted, network-supplied JavaScript code
file_indicators: Presence of node_logs.txt in system temp directory
Obfuscated or unusually large app.js file with benign exports and hidden malicious logic at the end
index.js that only launches pm2 with app.js as the target script
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests to ql.rustdesk.net or 62.234.32.226
Encrypted payloads in POST body to /api/index and /api/captcha endpoints

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages with postinstall scripts that launch pm2 or background daemons. Flag packages that create marker files in temp directories (e.g., node_logs.txt) and those that make periodic outbound HTTPS POST requests to suspicious or obfuscated domains, especially with encrypted payloads. Detect use of eval on decrypted network data. Analyze app.js files for obfuscated code and hidden logic at the end of otherwise benign files. Correlate network indicators such as connections to ql.rustdesk.net or 62.234.32.226 with the presence of AES-encrypted payloads and suspicious User-Agent strings.
